source: Jiang (2026) HindSight: Evaluating LLM-Generated Research Ideas via Future Impact
finding: Time-split test of idea quality: ideas made from pre-cutoff papers are matched to papers published later and scored by citations and venue. An LLM judge's novelty score was negatively related to this match, and the judge could not tell a retrieval-grounded generator from a plain one.
numbers: 200 ideas (100 retrieval-augmented ResearchAgent-style, 100 plain), Llama-3.3-70B generator, 10 AI/ML topics, 27,589 later papers (Jun 2023 to Dec 2025). Judge Qwen3-32B, 3 samples each. Judge overall 7.44 vs 7.40 (p=0.584). HindSight mean 0.297 vs 0.119 (p<0.001); match rate 81% vs 42%. Spearman of HindSight with judge novelty -0.291 (p=0.003), impact -0.225 (p=0.025), feasibility +0.252 (p=0.012), overall -0.075 (n.s.); all n.s. for the plain baseline.
quote: LLMs systematically overvalue novel-sounding ideas that never materialize
limits: Outcome is 'similar to a later published paper', not execution success. One generator family, one judge, small N, similarity threshold 0.96 chosen after looking (ratio 1.1x at 0.93 up to 3.8x at 0.965). Single-author preprint, not replicated.
agent_relevance: Best direct answer to gap 1: a cheap judge's novelty score ran against later real-world uptake, while a retrieval-grounded generator won on the outcome measure. Do not rank by judged novelty alone; add a time-split or outcome check where history exists.

source: Sternlicht, Shahid, Jansen, Weld, Siangliulue, Hope (2026) Old Ideas, Novel Problems: The Instability of LLM-Based Novelty Evaluation
finding: Controlled study of six LLM novelty judges against labels mined from OpenReview reviews (unanimous reviewer verdicts at the top and bottom decile). Small prompt edits flip verdicts and swing accuracy by 50+ points, and judges get worse and tie more once one side of the pair is LLM-generated.
numbers: Prompt change P3 to P4 (delete the sentence saying reviewers judged one idea novel) moves gpt-5.4 by 52.6 points on Human+Generated and the two prompts disagree on at least 52.6% of pairs (55.8% in practice). Same change moves claude-opus-4-6 21 points on Human-Only. Prompt change flips a quarter to a third of verdicts when ranking a stronger vs weaker ideation backbone, moving the share won by up to 29 points. Ties: up to 35% for claude-opus-4-6, over 50% for claude-sonnet-4-5.
quote: simply telling the judge that reviewers found one idea novel and the other not can change its verdict on more than half of the identical idea pairs
limits: Gold labels are reviewer text about novelty (noisy, and the lower-novelty side of Human+Generated is only weakly labelled). Not creativity in general; research ideas in AI only. Authors' own benchmark, preprint.
agent_relevance: A judge validated on one prompt, one data type or one backbone carries no guarantee elsewhere. Before using any judge we need a rated set drawn from our own generator, and we should log verdict flips under paraphrased prompts as a stability test.

source: Sternlicht et al. (2026) Old Ideas, Novel Problems (retrieval, reasoning, aggregation, dedicated judges)
finding: Retrieval, more reasoning and costlier purpose-built judges help little. Majority-of-3 aggregation helps a few points pointwise and more for pairwise judging. The cheapest prompted baseline beat both dedicated novelty evaluators.
numbers: Retrieval of 5 prior abstracts: significant gain of at most 16 points, only for some judges, never near 100; retrieval even significantly hurt some judges when the lower-novelty side came from other generators. Reasoning effort high to low: costs at most 7 points, often neutral. Removing the 3-call vote: pointwise changes mostly -0.3 to -4.7 points, pairwise up to -11.0 points; for gpt-5.4 pairwise Human+Generated the loss from P4 deepens from -37.0 to -46.8 and the gain from P3 shrinks from +15.6 to +12.3. Cheapest prompted setup beat Idea Novelty Checker and AI-Scientist judge by 8 to 29 macro-F1 points at up to 32x lower cost. A strong agentic search judge (gpt-5.6-sol, xhigh effort, arXiv search before 2025-03-01, unlimited tokens) did not beat standard retrieval.
quote: retrieval and larger reasoning budgets help little, and two purpose-built novelty evaluators are outperformed by our cheapest prompted baseline
limits: k=3 is the only aggregation size tested (no curve over k). Equal-token comparison against one long judgment was not run, but reasoning effort high-to-low (a large token cut) cost at most 7 points, which hints that tokens spent on one long judgment buy little.
agent_relevance: Partial answer to gap 3: a small vote (k=3) is worth a few points and more under pairwise judging; extra reasoning tokens and extra retrieval are not worth it. Spend the budget on repeated cheap calls with ties allowed, but the break-even k is still unmeasured.

source: Sternlicht et al. (2026) Old Ideas, Novel Problems (why retrieval misleads; style control)
finding: Retrieval can make a judge call an idea novel merely because none of five retrieved papers covers it, and can also make it dismiss a truly novel combination as 'a direct combination of existing ingredients'. Rewriting all ideas into one shared plan format did not remove the effects.
numbers: Case study of 22 gpt-5.4 correct-to-wrong flips caused by retrieval on pointwise Human+Generated; reading 10 cases (5 per class) where all 3 calls agree on each side. Style control: rewriting ideas into a shared plan format kept the direction of the largest prompt shifts, and instability grew (some changes flip over two thirds of examples; P4 costs gpt-5.4 24 points even on Human-Only).
quote: does not appear in the provided related work
limits: Qualitative sample of 10 cases. Retrieval pipeline may be weak (a stronger agentic retriever also did not help).
agent_relevance: Source-bounded novelty: the failure is 'absence from a small retrieved set counts as novelty'. Gap 6 and gap 7 both point to a rule: never accept novelty from absence in a bounded retrieved set; ask for the nearest prior and require code to check its overlap. Gap 4 for ideas: the instability is not a style artifact.

source: Du, Zhang et al. (2026) RINI: Seeing the Prior Is Not Enough
finding: Giving the model the earlier paper does not stop research proposals from claiming novelty for an established mechanism. An explicit step that audits each contribution claim against the evidence repairs many more cases than retrieve-and-revise or self-revision.
numbers: Human analysis of 175 interpretable exposed proposals: 137 recognized the prior's relevance, only 61 correctly attributed the established contribution; of 71 proposed remaining distinctions, 37 were covered by the same prior. On the same 240 originals needing correction (five annotators, 1,080 original-revision pairs): successful repair 11.7% self-revision, 39.1% retrieve-and-revise, 72.2% RINI, a 33.0 point gain over direct revision with the same evidence. Frozen corpus of 50,932 papers with a per-case date cutoff and exact paper version recorded.
limits: Measures claim attribution in proposals, not judge accuracy. Method and evaluation from the same team; whether annotators were blind to method is not stated in what I read. Preprint.
agent_relevance: Gap 6 and 7 for ideas: a source-boundedness check works when it is an explicit claim-by-claim attribution step, not 'here is the prior'. Also shows the cost of corpus choice is controllable by freezing the corpus and recording a per-case cutoff.

source: Chae, Kim, Jung, Choi, Jung (2026) Self- and Other-Labels Induce Bidirectional Bias in LLM Judges
finding: With style removed by design (judges score sets of narrative constraints picked from a shared pool) and authorship blind, the raw self-preference gap disappears once selection quality and judge severity are controlled. Authorship labels alone shift scores in both directions.
numbers: Ten LLMs as selectors and as judges, 200-constraint pool, 300 selections, 9,000 blind judging runs (3 repeats). Raw average self-preference S = +0.181 [0.13, 0.23]; after dropping the two low-discrimination judges S = +0.003 [-0.05, 0.06]; Originality stays slightly negative (-0.133 [-0.21, -0.05]). A random-slope model on all ten judges found no significant self-preference on any dimension. A leave-one-out k-NN could recover the source model at 50.7% (chance 10%), so each model has a signature. Experiment 2 (matched quality): self-labels raise scores 0.29 to 0.57 over other-labels on all four dimensions; all ten judges rate self-label above other-label; the label effect L is significant everywhere while true source A and interaction LA are not.
limits: Task is selecting narrative constraints, not judging finished ideas. Self-recognition was weak in blind mode, so this tests familiarity rather than recognition of a full text.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: self-preference by hidden authorship is near zero here; the strong effect is the label. In our pipeline, hide authorship and never tell the judge 'this is your idea'.

source: Chae et al. (2026) Self- and Other-Labels (research-proposal replication on the Si 2025 review form)
finding: Replication on full research proposals: ten models each wrote three proposals for three topics (90), style-normalized by a non-judge model (Claude Haiku 4.5), then judged blind and with self/other labels on matched pairs (85 pairs).
numbers: Label effect L on the Si 2025 review dimensions (row order read from Table 7): +0.196 (p<.001), +0.244 (p=.003), -0.116 (p=.016), +0.047 (p=.202), +0.206 (p<.001); actual-source effect and interaction not significant in the rows I could read.
limits: Direction of the label effect varies by dimension (one dimension reversed). Row-to-dimension mapping in my text extraction is partly garbled; use the paper's Table 7 before quoting a specific dimension. 90 proposals only.
agent_relevance: Idea-level confirmation of gap 5: with style normalized, authorship information, not content, drives the shift. Style-normalizing ideas before judging is a cheap guard.

source: Tutone, Franceschelli, Musolesi (2026) The Limits of Automatic Evaluation of Creativity in LLMs (full text)
finding: Blind human raters saw human and AI stories as nearly equal; a Llama-3.3-70B judge gave AI stories ceiling scores. The judge model did not write any of the stories, so this is machine-text preference, not own-output preference.
numbers: 200 WritingPrompts stories: 100 human, 100 machine (20 each from GPT-5.2, DeepSeek-V3.2, Mistral Large 3, Claude Sonnet 4.5, Gemini 3 Pro); 11 dimensions. Humans: only Authenticity (3.27 vs 3.50, p=.025) and Elaboration (3.17 vs 3.54, p=.005) differed. Judge: all 11 dimensions differed (mostly p<.001), with perfect 5.00 and zero variance on AI texts on several dimensions. Whole process blind.
limits: Story task, one judge model, 5-point scale ceiling. Elaboration was the one dimension humans also rated higher for AI text, so length and elaboration are not separated from the machine-text effect.
agent_relevance: Reconciles the Bhushan/Tutone conflict for gap 5: Tutone shows a bias for machine-style text from a judge that is not the author; Bhushan tests own-vs-other model with a neutral reference. Both can be true. For ideas (gap 4) it is still not tested whether removing elaboration removes the bias.

source: Bhushan, Zhang, Wang (2026) Can LLM Agents Discover? Evaluating Creativity on ML Engineering Tasks (full text, judge validation)
finding: Their judge validation tests self-preference by using a neutral judge on the generator's own outputs versus another generator's outputs. GPT-5 as judge was more conservative on its own agent runs.
numbers: Delta = GPT-5 score minus DeepSeek V3.2 score on all AIDE episodes: +0.300 for Qwen3-32B episodes vs +0.129 for GPT-5's own (p=0.000038), so GPT-5 does not inflate its own. Prompt ablation Spearman with human annotation: full prompt 0.732, no examples 0.684, no edge rules 0.699, no procedure 0.712. Position-in-run drift tests near zero (e.g. beta=+0.049, p=0.402).
limits: Judge scores ML agent trajectories against a rubric on code-run evidence, not ideas; one judge model; the neutral judge is itself one model. Not a hidden-authorship test of text.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: with a rubric over observable run evidence, no own-output inflation appeared. Rubric plus run history is the kind of cheap judge the gap asked about, but its target is human annotation, not later success.

source: Pombal, Rei, Martins (2026) Self-Preference Bias in Rubric-Based Evaluation of Large Language Models
finding: Even with fully objective rubrics (IFEval, LiveCodeBench), judges are more likely to wrongly pass criteria that the output fails when the output is their own. Majority-vote across judges lowers the bias but does not remove it.
numbers: Twelve judges; among rubrics where the generator fails, judges can be more than 50% more likely to mark them satisfied when the output is their own. On HealthBench, own-model bias skews scores by up to 10 points. Self-preference grows with output length quartile on HealthBench and LiveCodeBench; correlates with self-recognition and length, less with perplexity. A single judge overestimates its performance by about 4 points relative to an ensemble in one reported example.
limits: Not creativity tasks; no ideas. Blind-authorship condition not separated from recognizable-style condition in what I read.
agent_relevance: Gap 5 and gap 3: pooling several different judge models (not repeated samples of one) is the proven mitigation. Length drives the bias, so equalize length before judging.

source: Lyu, Kim, Xiao, Luan (2026) Why Large Language Models and Humans Converge and Diverge in Evaluating Creativity
finding: Six LLMs correlate moderately with trained human raters on ideas; broader evaluation standards align better; LLMs ignore social and market context that moves human ratings.
numbers: Study 2: 1,103 ideas, three trained raters averaged under CAT (ICC1=0.45, ICC2=0.71, median rWG=0.89). Mean of six LLMs vs human r=0.50. Individual models: GPT 0.52, Grok 0.49, DeepSeek 0.46, ERNIE 0.46, Claude 0.41, Gemini 0.41. Study 3: N=1,195 participants, 15 Kickstarter products; context sentence changed human ratings significantly but LLM ratings little.
limits: Human gold is rater opinion, not outcome. Ensemble of six different models (0.50) is within the range of the best single model (0.52), so pooling across models added little here.
agent_relevance: Gap 3 and gap 8: pooling six judge models did not beat the best single model; an agent judging ideas should expect r near 0.5 with trained-human consensus at best, and should not claim usefulness or market fit from a text-only judge.

source: Wang, Wu, Li, Zheng, Zhou (2026) Decoupled Analysis-Judging: An Automated Creativity Evaluator Using LLMs in Complex Multi-step Creativity Tasks (CreaEval)
finding: Splitting the judge into an evidence-extraction step and a separate scoring step gave much better agreement with expert scores than CoT, tree or graph reasoning, and than supervised fine-tuning on about 140 labelled samples. It also reduced length bias and score clustering at the top.
numbers: CGPST multi-step creativity task, 200 samples with two expert scores each. CreaEval QWK 0.64 (PCC 0.69, ICC 0.64); supervised fine-tuning of Qwen3.5-9B on a 7:3 split (about 140 training samples) QWK 0.47; training-free CoT, ToT, GoT, direct score and table-of-thought about 0.2 to 0.25. Ablations: no decoupling 0.21, no evidence step 0.24, extracting evidence for all six steps at once 0.01, no memory 0.49. Length-vs-Development-score correlation changed -5.81% for CreaEval, rose for CoT, GoT, ToT, and +0.82% for table-of-thought.
limits: One task family from the authors' own group, 200 samples, expert scores as gold. AUT and TTCW were also tested with gains (see Table 3 of the paper; I did not verify those cell values).
agent_relevance: Gap 3, 4 and 8: a structured two-stage rubric beat both longer reasoning and a 140-label fine-tune, so a small labelled set is not enough to train a judge but a decomposed rubric needs none. Length bias is reduced, not removed.

source: Ho, Liu, Nghiem et al. (2026) SoundnessBench: Can Your AI Scientist Really Tell Good Research Ideas from Bad Ones?
finding: Twelve frontier LLMs approve most research proposals that reviewers rated unsound. Aggressive prompting swaps false approvals for false rejections. A literature-grounded evaluator (ScholarEval) still approves two thirds.
numbers: 1,099 proposals (ICLR reviewer-derived proxy labels), 327 with proposal-only expert labels from 12 ML researchers. Standard prompt: mean low-soundness recall 26.0% (74.0% false-positive), high-soundness recall 91.8%. With expert labels: 64.8% false-positive. Aggressive prompt: false positives 19.9%, high-soundness recall 36.2% (26.7 to 33.0% on the expert subset); Macro F1 on expert labels 48.7% to 56.6%. ScholarEval at threshold 8.0: low recall 34.3%, high recall 73.3%, macro F1 53.7%, still approves 65.7% of unsound. Scale 2B to 35B raised high recall 71.8% to 92.8% and lowered low recall 31.0% to 19.2%.
limits: Soundness not novelty; proxy label is peer review, not execution. Optimism measured on ICLR submissions (a skewed set).
agent_relevance: Gap 7 for ideas: the same inflated-approval pattern as RQ-Bench's novelty mirage appears for soundness of proposals. Do not use an uncalibrated judge as a first gate; use a skeptical prompt only with a calibrated threshold on a rated set.

source: Wadhwa, Narayanan Venkit, Hayashi, Li, Chakrabarty, Wu (2026) Training Reasoning Models to Generate Diverse Scientific Ideas
finding: A set-level diversity objective raised idea diversity without lowering how often a coding agent could get a 'supports' verdict, within a small test. Diversity was measured with an LLM-rated distance that agrees with humans about as well as two humans agree with each other.
numbers: Human pilot: 4 PhD annotators, 15 instances each, 45 sets each. Promising ideas per set 2.17 (proposed) vs 2.20 (Claude Opus 4.8) vs 1.52 (Qwen3-8B); unique ideas 2.83 vs 2.72 vs 2.52. Execution: 132 ideas, 15 instances, 90 minute and $30 budget per idea; success@1/2/3 Claude 13/20/27%, proposed no-think 11/22/33%, proposed think 10/19/29%. Distance judge validation on 100 idea pairs: human-human Spearman 0.36, gpt-oss-120b 0.37, gemini-3.5-flash 0.50. A quality-diversity trade-off appeared in baselines (distance up, quality down).
limits: Tiny execution sample (15 instances, 3 ideas each); verdicts self-reported by an agent that the authors admit are sometimes stronger than the evidence; no per-idea correlation of diversity with success. Not NoveltyBench-style distinct-answer counting or semantic entropy.
agent_relevance: Gap 2 stays open: set-level diversity did not hurt execution success, and success rises with k (13 to 27%), which supports keeping several distinct ideas. It does not show that distinct count predicts which idea is useful.

source: Pei, Guo et al. (2026) DeepInstructor: An Agentic AI Instructor for Experience-Driven Idea Evaluation
finding: A judge that retrieves structured evidence from 58,607 peer reviews (an experience graph) improves agreement with human idea ratings over standalone LLMs and plain RAG, mostly on significance.
numbers: With ChatGPT-4o backbone: average Hit@1 and Hit@2 up 24.4% and 29.7% over standalone ChatGPT-4o on the Si 2024 expert-rated ideas (ExpertEval, 147 ideas). Standalone LLMs near floor on Significance (overly positive); passage-level RAG near zero Hit rate on Significance.
limits: Gold is human review scores, not execution. Relative gains quoted on top of low baselines. Built from ICLR 2024 and 2025 reviews, so dated.
agent_relevance: Gap 1 and gap 8: a rubric with history (past reviews) is a plausible cheap judge, but nobody has checked it against execution outcomes. Our agent's analogue is a per-task log of past ideas and outcomes.

source: Chen, Zhao, Cohan (2026) Measuring the Gap Between Human and LLM Research Ideas
finding: LLM ideas generated from the same prior papers cluster on 'bridge' opportunities and synthesis methods, a narrower and shifted distribution compared with the human papers.
numbers: Reference ideas reverse-engineered from high-quality papers plus their related prior works; ideas profiled on a two-axis taste taxonomy. Only the abstract and introduction were read in detail.
limits: Distribution gap, not quality; I read the abstract and introduction only.
agent_relevance: Gap 7 and gap 2: a narrowness signal (idea types concentrate) exists at the set level, which supports a code-side idea-type diversity check.

source: Chan et al. (2025) J1: Exploring Simple Test-Time Scaling for LLM-as-a-Judge
finding: Existing LLM judges do not improve when forced to think longer; the scaling trend appears only after RL training with verifiable rewards.
numbers: J1-7B beats the prior state of the art judge by 4.8% and shows a 5.1% stronger scaling trend under simple test-time scaling (appending 'Wait'). Three findings: existing judges lack the trend; SFT on reflection data still weak; trend emerges mainly in RL.
limits: Verifiable preference and math or code style judging, not creativity. I read the abstract, introduction and appendix A, not all tables.
agent_relevance: Gap 3 indirect: at fixed model, a longer single judgment has no reliable payoff; this agrees with Old Ideas (low vs high reasoning cost at most 7 points).

source: Xie, Ye, Zhang (2026) ALPS: Measuring Valid Creativity in Large Language Models with Mathematical Construction
finding: A benchmark for 'valid creativity' where a solution must be original and machine-checkable. It shows how to remove subjective judging by construction.
numbers: Each instance is one equational law needing either an infinite model or a proof of non-existence; 4,141-law evaluation pool; eight prover configurations resolve 2.2%; twentyfold budget adds 0.6%; strongest reasoning model 14% on proof side, none on construction side.
limits: Only mathematical tasks. No comparison of multi-criterion scores versus pass/fail inside this benchmark. I read the abstract, introduction and method parts.
agent_relevance: Gap 9 stays open for rating schemes: where a checker exists, pass/fail is the signal and nobody has shown Ritchie or SPECS-style scores add to it. Use checkable tasks to calibrate any softer judge.

source: Panickssery, Bowman, Feng (2024) LLM Evaluators Recognize and Favor Their Own Generations
finding: Self-preference in judges is linked to self-recognition: fine-tuning a judge to recognize its own text raised its self-preference in a linear trend, and the effect persisted after confound controls.
numbers: Summarization (XSUM, CNN/DailyMail), GPT-4, GPT-3.5, Llama-2; fine-tuning on 500 examples of self-recognition produced the trend; pairwise preferences reverse when source labels are reversed for some models and datasets.
limits: Summaries not ideas; the recognizable-authorship setting. Numbers beyond the 500-example fine-tune not re-read in full.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: self-preference needs recognizable style. Hiding authorship by normalizing style (as in Chae 2026) should remove most of it.
